The preceding section clarified the meaning of arising and ceasing as depending on causes and conditions.
Next, the following section reveals the essence and characteristics of the perfuming of causes and conditions.
This contains two parts.
First, the profound characteristics of dependent origination are briefly elucidated;
second, the various meanings of dependent origination are extensively revealed.
Within the first section, there are also two parts.
First, there is the brief indication praising its profundity;
second, the explanation of the reasons for its profundity.
This is the former.
The meaning of dependent origination has already been directly explained above.
What follows below again clarifies it by way of its profundity;
therefore, it says: "Furthermore, the perfuming of ignorance," and so forth.
The consciousness arising from the perfuming of ignorance identifies the substance of dependent origination;
that is, the intrinsically pure mind is the substance of dependent origination.

"The consciousness arising from the perfuming of ignorance" identifies the substance of dependent origination, which is the intrinsically pure mind; this refers to the totality of all deluded consciousnesses arising from ignorance.
This is called the consciousness arising from the permeation of ignorance;
it does not mean that one selectively grasps only the true or the delusory portions.
Regarding the phrase "not something that ordinary beings can know," etc.:
This is utterly beyond the reach of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding this fundamental principle of dependent origination,
ordinary beings possess the karma and afflictions that constitute the five abodes and the two obstacles.
Yet they cannot know it.
Although the followers of the two vehicles have realized it, because their wisdom is obstructed by the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), they are likewise unable to awaken to it.
It is precisely by virtue of this principle that...
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is extremely profound and subtle;
I do not reveal it to the foolish and the ignorant.
This means that from the level of the bodhisattvas downward, they know it only partially.
From the initial stage of correct concentration and faith, the bodhisattva gives rise to the resolve and engages in comparative observation;
reaching the stages of the bhūmis, they realize this bit by bit,
knowing that the causal true suchness (tathatā) follows conditions to form consciousness.
Since it can be both observed and realized, the Buddha taught this sutra.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse which says:
"Therefore, O Victorious One, I have revealed that which is called the ālaya."
Because the bodhisattvas have not yet completely severed the ground of ignorance (avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi),
their karma-consciousness (karma-vijñāna) has not perished;
this remains so even when they reach the tenth stage, the ultimate ground (niṣṭhā-bhūmi).
Furthermore, they have not yet fully understood the principle of dependent origination;
it is only the Buddha who has thoroughly realized it—
this clarifies that the Buddha is able to know it.
When ignorance is completely severed, the path of awakening becomes perfectly clear;

"Why is this? Because only a Buddha can know it. The commentary states:
This explains the meaning of its profundity.
The subtle principle of dependent origination permeates both the mundane and the sagely; only a Buddha exhaustively understands it.
Why is this so? The answer in the subsequent text consists of three sections.
The first clarifies that while there is purity, there is also constant defilement.
That this mind is inherently pure by its very nature means that,
according to its fundamental basis, it is the true mind of dependent origination which is original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*);
its own substance is undefiled and cannot be made pure by any separate purifying dharma.
Therefore, this collectively reveals the causal conditions for arising.
As for the presence of ignorance,
it means that based upon the essence of the mind, there is this ignorance as the condition of non-awakening.
This clarifies the conditions of dependent origination.
Regarding the statement that "one whose mind is defiled by ignorance has a defiled mind," it means that the essence of the mind is defiled by this ignorance.
Yet within the essence of the pure mind, there exists the defiled mind;
this reveals the characteristic of dependent origination.
In sum, this explains the scriptural passage concerning being "unstained yet stained."
Regarding the phrase "manifesting a defiled mind" and so forth:
it next clarifies that while being defiled, it is nonetheless eternally pure.
This means that although the fundamental awakened mind (mūla-awakening) is subject to defilement, [it remains inherently pure].
Although there is always a mind characterized by defilement, because its own nature is true,
it does not lose its fundamentally pure mental nature;
this explains the scriptural statement that "it is defiled, yet not defiled."
"Only the Buddha has fully realized it" means that the Buddha is able to know this principle because it is profound;
it is not something that others have fully realized.
The principle of dependent origination can be known only by a Buddha.
Thus, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states:
"The intrinsically pure mind is difficult to comprehend."
That mind, being defiled by afflictions,
is likewise difficult to discern.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
The Tathāgatagarbha is by nature pure;
it is only defiled by adventitious afflictions.
I shall now, together with you and all the bodhisattvas who possess profound wisdom, discern and distinguish this clearly.
Now, this treatise explains this [text] to reveal its profound depth.

This first section clarifies the causal conditions of ignorance (*avidyā*) within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The subsequent section clarifies the characteristics of the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) within dependent origination.

Regarding this initial point: although the aforementioned statement asserts that while there is a defiled mind it is eternally constant and unchanging, even though it is defiled, the defiled mind is itself eternally unchanging as it functions as the subject and object of cognition (*grāhaka-grāhya*).
Therefore, the defilement of thought is used to explain its immutability.
First, because its self-nature is eternally luminous and pure, it does not change;
yet it functions as the defiling agent of thought.
Second, because its intrinsic nature is not something that can be grasped, it does not undergo transformation;
thus, it acts as the defilement of what is contemplated.
Therefore, the *Xin lun* (New Treatise) states:
Although it may possess a defiled mind, it remains eternally luminous and pure,
without undergoing any change;
furthermore, this is because its fundamental nature lacks any discernible distinction.
Although it pervades all objective spheres,
it is without change;
though this passage is brief in wording, its meaning is complete.
Therefore, it is said that non-thought is called "unchanging.
The treatise states: "Because one does not penetrate [reality], it is called ignorance. The commentary explains:
This clarifies the reason for the dependent origination of ignorance (*avidyā*), based on the preceding explanation of the meaning of "having ignorance. According to one interpretation,
"non-attainment" is simply the absence of anything other than one's own mind.
Ignorance is defined as non-comprehension;
that is to say, because one does not personally realize the single flavor of equality,
it is not in accord with one's own fundamental mind.
It is called "ignorance" (avidyā) because there is no separate dharma [apart from it].
This is one interpretation.
It cannot contradict what was stated above,
because there is a defiled mind stained by ignorance;
and because there is a distinction between the characteristics of the causal conditions of the defiler and the defiled, as well as the resultant dependent origination.
If it were as previously stated—
that awakening is itself non-awakening—
then one would incur the same faults that were refuted earlier.
If it is argued that ignorance is so called because it is dissociated from the mind,
then the three preceding afflictions would necessarily be states of awakening,
since they are associated with the mind.
Consequently, there exists a distinct ignorance capable of causing delusion;
although it is not separate from reality, it is also not identical to the essence of reality.
It is an extremely subtle delusion of the mind that fails to realize the thought-free *dharmadhātu*.
This should properly be called "dissociated from mind" (*cittaviprayukta*),
because there has not yet been a distinction between the subject (the sovereign) and its mental factors (the attendants).
It is called "mind-dissociated" (*citta-viprayukta*) due to an inversion in the phrasing.
This does not mean that they are dissociated from their respective portions.
Therefore, the *Xinlun* (New Treatise) states:
"Because they do not realize the single Dharma-realm, they are dissociated."
Ignorance arises from discrimination; it alone can serve as the source of all defilements, for there is no other root of defilement.
Therefore, it is said that "thoughts arise suddenly. The Sūtras speak of the five abodes.
Because no other distinct dharma arises prior to it, it is called the "beginningless ground of abiding ignorance" (*anādikālikāvidyāvāsabhūmi*).
To clarify that there is no separate dharma that constitutes the beginning of ignorance is precisely the meaning of this treatise regarding its "sudden arising."
This is explained according to the gate of mutual dependence between the subtle and the coarse;
it is not according to temporal sequence, because there is no beginning to their arising.

"Defiled minds are of six kinds. Commentary:
Next, the characteristics of the dependent origination of defiled minds are revealed.
This section contains two parts.
This is the first part, providing a general heading followed by a detailed explanation.
It specifically comments upon the preceding phrase: "the mind that is defiled by ignorance and possesses defilement."
Regarding the statement that ignorance defiles the mind with defilement,
there are six types: namely,
the aforementioned mental consciousness and the five kinds of mental faculties.
Previously, the meaning of dependent origination was explained;
therefore, the questions were addressed in sequence from the subtle toward the coarse.
Now, because I wish to simultaneously clarify the meaning of its treatment and abandonment, [I shall proceed as follows].
From the coarse to the subtle, they are clarified in successive order;
thus, although they appear before and after one another, there is no distinction between them.

"What are the six [factors] for the sake of distancing oneself? The commentary states:
Next, the six defilements are explained, which are divided into six parts.
This grasping associated with [the mind] is precisely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is also, among the six types of coarseness, the coarse characteristic of grasping at names and conceptualizing meanings within the four characteristics;
for it is increased by the afflictions of views and craving.
Because the coarse attachments such as "I" and "mine," when associated with them, are contrasted with defiled and pure minds,
they are termed "defilement associated with attachment.
This explains the obstacles and thereby reveals their antidotes.

If practitioners of the two vehicles reach the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and sever the afflictions of both views and cultivation, they are able to remain free from this defilement; when Bodhisattvas enter and abide in this stage, their signs of faith are perfected and there is no further regression—this is called "correspondence with faith" (*śraddhā-samprayukta*).
Therefore, both the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the treatises of Asaṅga state that the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi are called the Stage of Practice through Faith (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Within this stage, although one has not yet attained the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the afflictions of attachment and craving (*rāga-kleśa*) cannot manifest.
Therefore, "remote" does not mean that the seeds of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have not yet been eliminated.
Why, then, would the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) not be severed at this stage? According to one interpretation:
Because the power of the path prior to the stages (bhūmi) is inferior,
present afflictions are liable to arise;
how much less could it sever their seeds?

Upon reaching the first bhūmi, one attains the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and only then severs the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that are conceptually constructed; however,
one retains the seeds of those that are innate (*sahaja*) in order to assist the practice of taking birth.
Because they are only permanently severed upon attaining Buddhahood,
the seeds of the objects of knowledge are suppressed and severed stage by stage,
until they are finally and completely exhausted at the stage of Buddhahood.
Therefore, [it is argued that] before the stages of the Path of Seeing (bhūmi), the seeds of the afflictions are not severed.
According to one interpretation, this explanation is not yet fully clear in its reasoning.
However, because it accords with the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) according to the Mahāyāna meaning,
a Bodhisattva at the stage of faith (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) is able to attain the Buddha-body and manifest the eightfold path of enlightenment (aṣṭābhisambodhi).
Since they perform the work of transforming sentient beings and are also able to perceive, even partially, the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*),
how is it that they cannot sever the seeds of the afflictions?
One is able to give rise to the supreme path to permanently sever the afflictions;
however, fearing that this might obstruct one's practice and vows, the seeds of delusion are retained.
Therefore, the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states accordingly:
If one does not sever the higher [defilements], one is no different from ordinary beings;
if one does not retain the seeds [of those defilements], one is no different from the followers of the Two Vehicles.
For the sake of benefiting oneself and others, one retains the seeds of delusion.
Furthermore, one does not fear delusion,
because one knows that True Suchness (tathatā) manifests through conditions without ever differing from its true nature.
One takes afflictions as the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), knowing that they are like emptiness manifested by transformation.
Because the disciples' various afflictions are maintained according to their own will;
once they reach the stage of the Grounds, they sever only the cognitive obscurations and no longer remain subject to the afflictive obscurations.
There is no distinction between what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation, nor between seeds and manifest states,
because they lack the power [to function] and serve no purpose; furthermore,
since the auxiliary practices and the taking of rebirth do not necessarily require this [power].
If there are residual habitual tendencies,
they are severed only upon attaining Buddhahood;
therefore, it is said in the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
Because all afflictive hindrances obstruct the practice of benefiting sentient beings,
one completely abandons the afflictions of the *manas* simultaneously within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, because the power of one's vows is superior from the very first stage (*bhūmi*), one does not fall into the levels of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Furthermore, it is not only that the afflictions of the four stages of abiding are severed,
but one can also partially sever the stage of abiding in ignorance;
therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
Those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm observe and study its abandonment from the stage of "conformity with faith"; here,
however, we merely reveal the coarse attachments and defilements.
Treatise:
Second, because it is uninterrupted until reaching ultimate detachment. Commentary:
This refers to what is called the "continuing consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*) among the five types of mental intention.
Among the six preceding defilements, it is called the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*).
The continuity of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is termed non-interruption (*anuccheda*).
That which can defile the pure mind is termed uninterrupted defilement (*anuccheda-kleśa*).

The Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness cultivate the study of consciousness-only and, through the investigation of reality and true wisdom, gradually subdue such conceptual attachments to phenomena by means of various contemplations.
Upon entering the [first] stage, they realize the three natures of non-essence.
Because both the manifest and the seeds of the conceptualization that clings to dharmas have perished,
it is said that one attains the ultimate detachment of the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*).
The initial attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state is designated as "Pure Mind."
It is not the pure mind of a subsequent stage.
The treatise states: "Third, because it is distinguished by reaching the ultimate state of detachment. The commentary explains:
Within the five mental activities, it is termed "cognition of wisdom" (jñāna-vijñāna).
Within the six defiled states, it is termed the "characteristic of wisdom" (jñāna-lakṣaṇa).
That which discriminates between the defiled and the pure is termed "distinctive wisdom" (viśeṣa-jñāna).
Because it defiles the pure mind, it is called "affliction.
From the second stage through the sixth stage,
one does not abide for long in untainted contemplation.
Because there are subtle distinctions among the objects encountered upon emerging from meditative observation,
this attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) has not yet been permanently abandoned.
Nevertheless, because it can be eliminated bit by bit at each stage when entering meditative observation, it is said to be "gradually abandoned."
If one reaches the seventh stage and enters meditative absorption for a long duration,
such that these [defilements] never again arise, this is called "ultimate detachment.
This refers to the stage of possessing ethical discipline (*śīla*).
This refers to the second bhūmi,
because this stage is fully endowed with the three clusters of ethical discipline (tri-śīla-saṃvara).
The skillful means regarding signlessness (animitta-upāya) refers to the seventh bhūmi.
This is because one constantly dwells with mental attention on signless contemplation;
it does not mean that the eighth stage is the cause of signlessness.
Those who explain it in this way are all providing erroneous interpretations.
What is stated in the *New Treatise* regarding the progression from the stage of complete precepts (*śīla*) to the stage of complete wisdom (*prajñā*):
one who is partially separated [from the former] reaches the sixth stage and is termed "possessing complete wisdom.

This is because they possess the superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) associated with the contemplation of the truths of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) throughout the preceding three stages.
Treatise:
Fourth, because manifest form can be detached from. Commentary:
Among these five types of mind, this is the third, the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
The first three among the subtle [transformations] are the aspect of objective realms (*viṣaya-nimitta*).
Because they manifest forms and images like a clear mirror,
and because they can defile the pure mind, they are called "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*).
Because one attains the three masteries (*vaśitā*) within the eighth stage, such that the nature of form follows the mind without obstruction,
the eighth stage is called "Mastery over Form.
One is thus able to realize mastery over marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and lands (*kṣetra*).
The manifestation of the body and land of True Suchness (tathatā) arises from the six [sense bases].
Delusory objects of ignorance are forever severed from this;
therefore, it is said that this stage can eliminate the defiled manifestations.
Treatise:
Fifth, because it is able to see up to being able to detach. Commentary:
Among these five types of mind, this refers to the second, the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Among the three subtle states mentioned above, it is the "characteristic of the perceiving subject" (*nengjian-xiang*).
The moving mind (*dongxin*), which serves as the basis, transforms into the perceiving subject.
That which defiles the pure mind is termed "defilement" (*ran*).
In the ninth stage, one attains unimpeded wisdom;
through skillfully knowing the dense forest of the mental activities of sentient beings with sovereign non-obstruction,
it is called "mastery over the mind."
Because that which possesses obstruction can never arise when taking this as its object,
it is said that the "ground of mastery over mind" (*cittavaśitā-bhūmi*) is able to transcend it.
Furthermore, unobstructed wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*) is briefly of four types and extensively of forty types.
As stated elsewhere in the treatise:
"Sixth, the fundamental [attainment] up to the ability to abandon. The commentary says:
This is what is called the "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*) among the five mental states;

Each has its own description, yet they do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, when attachment and so forth all function as the self, their activity and resolution take [the object] as a condition; this is what is called "knowing the same.

because this consciousness arises depending on an object, it corresponds with that object.

"Mind" refers here to the cognizing mind.

although these latter three defilements are also agitated minds,

how could there be the sense of "knowing together" or "taking the same object"? Therefore, it is said that they do not know each other's characteristics or take each other's characteristics as objects.

If that is so, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that the ālayavijñāna is associated with the mental factors (*caitta*)?
Answer: This is based on the principle of subtle interpenetration.
The mind and non-awakening (abodha) are conjoined such that they appear as one and cannot be distinguished;
because they have not yet become differentiated, there is no defiled mental factor (caitta) called "dissociated" (viprayukta).
That [system] establishes the existence of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) based on a coarse and superficial principle of exposition.
Because they arise together with the mental factors that are omnipresent (sarvatraga), they achieve association (saṃprayoga).
Each relies on its own specific object, and thus there is no contradiction.
Regarding the reliance on the mind as the object:
This means that this moving mind is, in its very essence, non-awakening;

Because non-awakening exists right within the moving mind,

This is not the same as [discussing] the characteristic of knowing or the characteristic of being conditioned.
Because it is briefly associated with the preceding [mental factors],

If this were the case, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) should not manifest objects.

That is to say, within the coarse and superficial gateway of the Dharma-characteristics school (*lakṣaṇavāda*), the one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion, which take the grasping at a self as their primary cause, torment sentient beings and obstruct nirvāṇa; these are called the "affliction-obstructions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Taking the attachment to phenomena as primary, the views, doubt, ignorance, craving, pride, and so forth, which obscure the objects of knowledge and obstruct enlightenment, are termed the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These two types of obstructions are definitively present in the seven distinct consciousnesses.
It does not coexist with the eighth consciousness.
Within the secret gate of the Faxing school,
it is not merely that the two attachments and two obstacles exist within consciousness.
Taken together with those eight consciousnesses, they are collectively termed the "fundamental ignorance of affliction.
Because it is subtle and because it serves as the basis [for all other afflictions], it is called the "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Its abandonment constitutes liberation.
Because of this distinct meaning, the term "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) is employed.
For this reason, "obstruction" (*pratighāta*) and "hindrance" (*āvaraṇa*) are distinct. According to another interpretation:
This argument is necessarily untenable. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* names them "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*) but does not speak of "impediments" (*pratighāta*).
Therefore, works such as the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* also employ the term "impediment" based on the tenets of the former school.
How could this be considered a concealment?
The translator has merely placed obstacles [in the text] without distinction;
one can only clarify the depth or shallowness of the meaning according to the specific school's tenets.
Regarding the phrase "defiled mind," the statement that "the six kinds of defiled minds can obstruct" clarifies its meaning as being an impediment.
The wisdom that illuminates tranquility and accords with reality is called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
In this term "fundamental wisdom," both interpretations— that the fundamental is the wisdom, or that it is the wisdom of the fundamental— are equally valid.
This is precisely what was referred to above as the "characteristic of the purity of wisdom.
This fundamental wisdom is called "true thusness" (tathatā) because it is the wisdom of the original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) of true thusness itself.
Second, because they arise through cultivation based upon true suchness (*tathatā*).

These are the obstacles consisting of the defiled mind’s weariness, affliction, and agitation.

ignorance and delusion lack any discernment;
to oppose the function of this wisdom is termed "obstruction to knowledge" (jñeyāvaraṇa).

Regarding the statement "the pervasive ceases," this means that when the antidote to ignorance is attained and ignorance itself ceases, the objective realm of the manifest consciousness that arose [in dependence upon it] also ceases accordingly; therefore,

Within the gate of arising and ceasing, the true suchness of original enlightenment internally perfumes ignorance, causing one to develop weariness with and a quest for [samsara], thereby turning away from defilement and clarifying the truth;

"By the power and conditions of the future Buddha-nature, one again gives rise to wholesome retribution.

Question:
As explained in various treatises, the perfuming agent (kṣobhaka) and the perfumed object (kṣobhya) each possess four characteristics before they can be termed "perfuming" (vāsanā).
What are these four characteristics of the perfumed object?
1. The nature of firm abiding;
2. the nature of being indeterminate;
3. the nature of being susceptible to perfuming.
Fourth, it possesses the nature of being in common conjunction with the perfuming agents (*bhāvakas*).
There are four types of perfuming agents:
first, those that possess arising and ceasing.
Second, it possesses superior efficacy;
third, it possesses intensification;
fourth, it evolves in conjunction with that which is perfumed.
Since true suchness (*tathatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and other eternal phenomena have already been excluded,
why is it said here that true suchness is both the perfumer (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*)? Answer:
This is because there are three meanings that do not contradict one another.
First, since perfuming (*vāsanā*) is conceivable,
various treatises provisionally explain to those of the initial capacity that this perfuming of arising and ceasing is conceivable.
This treatise reveals that for those of long-standing faculties, the inconceivable perfuming of the eternal dharma is also taught.
Because there are two true gates regarding the perfumer and the perfumed,
various treatises provisionally speak only of the immovable *tathatā*.
Because it is not that which produces [phenomena], it is neither the perfumer nor the object of perfuming.
This treatise, however, establishes it as both the perfumer and the object of perfuming because True Suchness (tathatā) arises in accordance with defilement by following conditions.
Third, because the dharma of True Suchness is not fixedly eternal.
Various treatises explain that *tathatā* (suchness) is permanent based on the principle of formal establishment;
it is neither the perfuming agent nor the object of perfuming.
This treatise, however, also relies upon the principle of perfect interfusion.
It is not that True Suchness (tathatā) is exclusively either the single perfuming agent or the single object of perfuming;

rather, each is established according to its own specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another. If one were to say that True Suchness is definitively permanent and definitively unitary, [it would be a contradiction].
This would then be identical to the *ātman* (self) as conceived by non-Buddhists;
however, because it is neither fixed, permanent, nor unitary, there is no fault in its being perfumed (*vāsana*).

Generally speaking, there are three meanings of perfuming:

which perfumes the false and increases delusion.
Third, the perfuming of the three resources:
this perfuming causes delusion and gives rise to attachment,
which is what is meant by "ignorance depending on the true."
This refers to the substance of ignorance as it is subsequently perfumed.
Because the delusive phenomena of ignorance cannot establish themselves independently,
it is said that ignorance exists in dependence upon the True.
"Because there is ignorance, that very ignorance immediately permeates the True [Mind]" refers to the meaning of fundamental ignorance as a concealing and permeating agent.
"Because of this permeation, there is the deluded mind."
Based on the permeation of ignorance, there truly exists the mind of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
This briefly clarifies the meaning of the permeation of ignorance.
As for "because there is a deluded mind, even up to the manifestation of deluded objects":
This reveals that the habitual perfuming of the deluded mind causes ignorance to increase its lack of understanding and its deviation from true equality,
thereby giving rise to the evolving consciousnesses; hence it is said that "non-awakening gives rise to thoughts."
Furthermore, because the manifest consciousness arises, one speaks of "manifesting delusive objects.
This briefly clarifies the meaning of the deluded mind's perfuming.
As for the statement that "delusive objects perfume the deluded mind," etc.:
This clarifies that the objective realm acts as a conditioning influence upon the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), causing it to give rise to attachment and the commission of karma.

This means that when objects arise, they stir the ocean of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), giving rise to the waves of the six coarse object-consciousnesses (*vastu-vijñāna*) and causing them to become attached to various delusive objects.
"Combining" refers to the phase of intellection (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the phase of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*);
both of these are instances of the conceptualization of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
"Attachment" means grasping or clinging.
This is the characteristic of name-and-form.
These two—both being attached to "self" and "mine"—thereby create various kinds of karma;
this is precisely the characteristic of the activity of cognition.
From ignorance through to this arising of karma,
all of these constitute the original cause and are thus the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
As for "experiencing all sufferings of body and mind," etc.:
That is to say, the characteristic of suffering bound by karma constitutes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
These points briefly clarify the meaning of the permeation of objects.
In this section of the *New Treatise* (*Xinlun*), the phrasing and meaning are somewhat sparse and brief.
If that is so, why not say that the objects are perfumed by delusion? Answer:
What is revealed here is that delusion arises from the True [Nature].
Regarding the cycle of birth and death, it is said that there are three types of perfuming;
once the subtle and coarse delusions have already brought about this cyclic existence,
the perfuming of the deluded mind upon objects serves no further purpose.
Objects are merely what is manifested by the mind;

because objects do not arise through the熏 (xūn— perfuming) of delusion.

What is called the "limb of the grasping at a self through conventional designation" (nāma-vikalpa-ātma-grāha-aṅga) consists of two types of conventional designation:
that which expresses meaning and that which reveals objects.
Because of these perfumed seeds, the causes and conditions are distinct.
There are two types of self-grasping:
the innate and the conceptual.
Due to this perfuming, there is a distinction between self and others.
There are two types of links of existence:
wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Due to these, the seeds are perfumed, resulting in the differentiation between the realms of suffering and bliss.
Regarding whether these [seeds] are identical to or different from these three [types of existence],
this is explained according to the gateway of the profound and subtle meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The *ālaya* also possesses the capacity to be perfumed.
Regarding its state as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), three types of perfuming are taught.
Those [three] are explained solely in terms of the principle of coarse and superficial dependent origination, taking the phenomenal consciousness (*saviṣayavijñāna*) as their essential nature.
These three types are explained in the context of the consciousness of objects;
it is precisely due to these three kinds of perfuming within this state that they draw forth the fundamental consciousness to produce the fruits of the five destinies.
Although the coarse and the subtle differ, they together constitute birth and death.
Herein, the meaning of perfuming the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is explained in detail, while the event-consciousness (*sadvijñāna*) is briefly indicated,
as it is coarse and thus easy to understand.
This treatise explains only the meaning of the three types of perfuming— namely, the object-consciousness and so forth— within the context of the Vijñapti-mātra (consciousness-only) system,
because it proceeds according to the principle of ultimate reality.

Because this consciousness possesses fundamental ignorance and does not realize the signless dharma of suchness,

"Because the fundamental consciousness arises appearing as the sense organs, objects, self, and consciousness,
there are two types of objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness."
First, it appears as the objective realm of distinct, real dharmas;
second, it appears as the objective realm of a general, real self.
Due to the power of the perfuming of these dharma-resemblances, the characteristics of that cognition and its continuity arise.
Because this is precisely the notion of dharma-attachment within the active consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), it is said that "the perfuming of the increase of notions" occurs.
Due to the power of the perfuming of the object that resembles a self,
there arise the characteristic of grasping and the characteristic of calculating names.

If that were so, the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* would have to grasp external objects.
Because there is no objective realm consisting of images transformed by oneself. Answer:
In reality, there is indeed an objective realm transformed by oneself.
Because both objects transformed by these two consciousnesses possess the sense of arising from mind and giving rise to mind,
just as the evolving and manifesting consciousnesses give rise to various objective realms,
it is precisely through these manifesting objects that the evolving and manifesting consciousnesses are established.
Because the objective realm draws forth mental aspects that manifest within consciousness,
the grasping at a self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyagrāha*) manifests with the self of phenomena as its object.
This is because the grasping at a self of phenomena and its objective realm are established in mutual dependence as the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).
In this passage, only the arising of the mind is discussed;
it does not speak of the objective realms manifested by the *pravṛtti-vijñāna*.
This is intended to clarify the manifestation of objects.

Furthermore, because they perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and cause the arising of the phenomenal consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) through the grasping of the notions of phenomena and self,

"Because the perfuming of the deluded mind leads to the suffering bound by karma. The commentary states:
This is an extensive elaboration of the preceding discussion on the perfuming of the deluded mind;
it provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of the deluded mind’s perfuming of ignorance.
The deluded mind is twofold: the karmic consciousness and the phenomenal consciousness.
Therefore, there are two types of meanings regarding the perfuming of the deluded mind.
The deluded mind of karmic consciousness is able to permeate the fundamental ignorance, which in turn becomes confused regarding the signless.
This gives rise to the evolving aspect and the manifesting aspect in continuous succession,
thereby forming the essential characteristics of the various sufferings of rebirth.
Although those of the three vehicles have emerged from the triple world and abandoned the coarse suffering of the segmented consciousness (*prātibhajñāna*),
because this fundamental root-consciousness remains, they still experience the *pariṇāma* (transformation) and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) within the ālayavijñāna.
Speaking generally, they have existed since beginningless time; however,
for the purpose of distinguishing the subtle from the coarse, they are discussed here.
Approximately at the stage when one has departed from coarse suffering, it is said that the deluded mind of the phenomenal consciousness (*saviṣaya-vijñāna*) is perfumed;
through the activation of ignorance— the branches and twigs of views and craving— one initiates various karmas by means of body and speech,
thereby forming the "mark of initiating karma" (*karma-samutthāna-lakṣaṇa*) capable of summoning [birth within] the three realms.
Ordinary beings and those still in training experience the suffering of manifold activities and the coarse suffering of segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*).
Regarding these two types of suffering, various teachings offer different explanations;
if one follows the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they refer to the segmented birth-and-death.
With contaminated karma as the cause and the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) as the condition,

the coarse resultant fruits (*vipākaphala*) of the three realms— which are to be extinguished— such as the body and lifespan being long or short, are fixed and severed according to the power of their respective causes and conditions.
Therefore, it is called "segmented" (paricchinna).
This applies to ordinary beings, the two vehicles of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage,
because they possess, as appropriate, the causes of those afflictions and karma.
Because the grasping at "I" and "mine" has not been exhausted,
because the afflictions of the manas have also not been severed,
and because the designation "ālaya" has still not been relinquished.

Therefore, as long as one has not yet transcended the coarse suffering of the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) death and rebirth and the inconceivable *pariṇāma-cyuti* (transformation) death and rebirth,
one takes uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma involving conceptual differentiation as the cause and the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as the contributory condition.

The extraordinary, subtle, and superior fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) that is extinguished is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) because, through the power of compassion and vows, the physical body and life-span have no fixed limit.
It is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*) because its wondrous function— being properly sustained and extinguished by untainted meditative concentration and vows— is difficult to fathom.
It is also called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*),
because it is accomplished according to one's mental vows; it is also called the "transformation body" (*nirmāṇa-kāya*),
because the power of untainted concentration transforms it so that it differs from its original state, just like a magical creation.

This supernormal power is not fixed, as it is possessed by those in the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning, as well as by Bodhisattvas on the eighth stage and above who, through their great vows, act for the benefit and happiness of others;
yet, because the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) obstructs great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
Because they have already permanently severed and subdued the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) while maintaining their physical bodies for a long duration,
there is no possibility that they would receive a future body subject to the divisions of death and rebirth;
this is because they fear it would interrupt their long-term cultivation of the bodhisattva practices.
By means of the power of aspiration from untainted, supreme meditative concentration, one sustains the causes for manifesting the present body with dharmas such as those [previously mentioned],
causing them to yield their fruits without interruption over a long period.
In this manner, one repeatedly receives the assistance of such concentration and aspiration.
Until the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi,
one undergoes the birth-and-death of transformation (pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa) because of this.
If one explains this meaning by means of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā):
Due to the perfuming of fundamental ignorance, the karmic consciousness arises;
subsequently, the evolving and manifesting consciousnesses arise, perfumed by karma and ignorance,
thereby constituting the essence of the ālayavijñāna within the cycle of birth and death.
Yet these are not yet designated as the bitter fruits of the five destinies.
Because the fundamental ignorance perfumes and gives rise to the phenomenal consciousness (*samsarika-vijnana*),
and this consciousness perfumes and gives rise to views and craving, which in turn produce good and evil karma.
Drawing forth the ālayavijñāna,
it brings about the fruits of the five destinies;
only then does one become bound by the karma of an ordinary person and experience coarse suffering.
All ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles who are still in training, and all bodhisattvas who have not yet ascended to the stages (bhūmi),
according to their respective capacities, have not yet severed the coarse afflictions of views and craving.

Because they are extinguished by the coarse karma and afflictive karma arising from the perfuming of the phenomenal consciousness (*vṛtti-vijñāna*), they experience the coarse fruits of the three realms.
Ordinary beings experience coarse suffering bound by their karmic actions;
however, when those of the two vehicles reach the stage of no-more-learning,
or when Bodhisattvas attain entry into the first bhūmi, they have permanently severed or suppressed the coarse and subtle afflictions.
Because he has severed all coarse outflows of karma,
he does not receive a coarse body within the three realms; thus,
although he is able to forever leave behind the coarse suffering of ordinary beings, [he remains].
Because subtle ignorance has not yet been severed;
because the subtle consciousness it gives rise to still continues;
and because uncontaminated subtle karma has also not yet been relinquished.
It is the natural law that there is a subtle continuity of suffering.
The Sūtras state that those on the first bhūmi attain the body of mental mastery (*manomaya-kāya*);
this is because those of the two vehicles possess three types of understanding.
It does not mean that one intentionally arouses an untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and aspiration to provide the cause for transforming the present body; rather,
it means that by manifesting true thusness (*tathatā*) as being subtly free from coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Therefore, it is called "transformation.
When the defilements of ignorance are thin and true virtue is manifested, such that one can spontaneously engage in activity,
this is termed the accomplishment of the inconceivable mental body (*manomaya-kāya*).
There is no logical flaw here.
Although those dwelling in the initial stage are sustained by the power of their superior vows and are not bound by karma,
they appear to be free from coarse suffering.
Because it is associated with subtle suffering due to contaminated karma,
it differs from the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the higher stages. Alternatively,

Answer: It is the path capable of transformation, abiding in the family of the Tathāgatas, and being born into the assembly of the Buddha’s gathering.
Having already been able to perceive a small portion of the Dharma-body,

Since they are alike in being on the ground and also free from coarse suffering,
there is no contradiction in explaining that those who first attain the body of mental mastery (manomayakāya) are further described as such to emphasize this point.
As it is said that one perceives the root-body only from above the ground,

Let us set aside this digression and return to the explanation of the main text.
If it is claimed that the event-consciousness (samsaric consciousness) perfumes the views and attachments,
why is it stated both before and after that this consciousness is increased by the afflictions of views and attachments? Answer:
Because both of these two kinds of deluded minds— the coarse and the subtle— possess the meaning of being "dependent on others" and "forming others.
That is to say, the preceding karmic consciousness is established in dependence upon ignorance,
and it in turn serves as the support and sustenance for ignorance.
Because delusion gives rise to the false, and one abides based on that falsity;
if there were no falsity, there would be no basis for abiding,
as the intrinsically pure *tathatā* (suchness) is not a place of abiding.
Because it perfumes the true [nature] to give rise to the false and acts as its dwelling place,
that which is called the *karmic-result consciousness* (ālayavijñāna) arises based upon the perfuming of the true nature by views and craving;
it is further able to habitually perfume views, craving, and ignorance to give rise to various karmas and so forth.
Because the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and the mind-state (*cittasthiti*) mutually support one another, there is no contradiction:

what was previously explained as the "other-dependent" (*paratantra*) is here referred to as the "perfuming that establishes the other" (*pariniṣpanna-paratantra*), specifically in terms of the views and cravings that arise from such perfuming.
Thus, the two are not inconsistent.
In this context, the karmic consciousness is called the "root" because it arises directly dependent upon fundamental ignorance and because it is the primary source of all deluded minds.
The "discriminative consciousness of objects" (vastuprativikalpavijñāna) is called "increasing" because it is increased by the afflictions of views and craving, and because it,
in turn, can increase those afflictions of views and craving.
Treatise:

This extensively explains the aforementioned meaning of the perfuming of concealment.
This extensively explains the meaning of the perfuming of True Suchness by ignorance (*avidyā*).

there are two types of the meaning of its perfuming.
The "subtle" refers to the ground of abiding fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*);

as it is the root of the four external abidings (*catur-āśraya*).
This [ignorance] can obscure and permeate the unmoving True Suchness,
causing it to move delusively and thereby form the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). This, in turn,
can give rise to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).
Now, because we are citing only the beginning, it is called "mental karma" (citta-karma).
"Coarse" refers to the four abidings and ignorance at the level of branches and subordinates;
these are precisely the views and attachments that arise within this context.
Since the afflictions of attachment to views and craving arise from the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āvasthā*),
they are able to obscure and permeate the already-arisen True Suchness (*tathatā*) so that it undergoes transformation.
Furthermore, because coarse and active consciousnesses accomplish their respective functions,
the preceding text states:
"This consciousness increases by depending on the afflictions of views and craving."
These two types of ignorance also have two meanings.
That is to say, fundamental ignorance can permeate true suchness (tathatā) to produce karma, transformation, and so forth;
and because it abides in dependence upon karma and the like, it sustains delusion, and because it exists based on delusion, it is established as false.
At its conclusion, ignorance perfumes and gives rise to the phenomenal consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*),
which abides in dependence upon that phenomenal consciousness; for the sovereign [storehouse consciousness] and the mental factors apprehend their objects in mutual dependence.
In this context, it is explained for the purpose of establishing the position of others that ignorance perfumes the karmic consciousness and so forth.

because the essence of the mind is manifested through the cause of realization, it is called attaining nirvana.

The treatise states: "Because the perfuming of the deluded mind leads most swiftly to the attainment of nirvāṇa. The commentary explains:

Because true permeation gives rise to the wisdom that acts as the permeating agent based on the two deluded minds, it is said that the meaning of deluded permeation is twofold;

Because this arises from ignorance, it merely serves as a supporting condition for wisdom (*jñāna*) and is said to be able to permeate wisdom (*vāsana*); however, this "ability to permeate" does not mean that it is itself the permeation.

There is an interpretation that these two delusions are themselves the capacity [for perfuming], because they arise from being perfumed by True Suchness; thus,
their meaning stands in opposition to the meaning of perfuming by ignorance.
Because the functions of the deluded minds that arise are each distinct,

If it were not so, then true permeation would not differ from ignorance;

Since that is not the case,

The principle is indeed thus.

Furthermore, if such were the case, from what would these two types of wisdom arise?
If it were derived solely from the true, it should not be called false;
since it is termed false,

Therefore, because what was previously stated is profoundly untenable,
these two delusions are able to permeate the True [Mind].
They possess no separate substance from the wisdom of aversion and seeking.
Based on this wisdom, one should formulate four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) regarding delusion. There is that which is delusion but not wisdom;

That which is wisdom and not delusion is called the illuminating function of *tathatā* emerging from ignorance;

that which is both existence and both delusion and wisdom is called that which arises through being perfumed by *tathatā*; that which is neither existence nor delusion and neither wisdom nor non-wisdom is [the ultimate].
This means that because it is the rational nature manifested by the gate of True Suchness (tathatā),

If one provides this interpretation,

This argument is also untenable,

Question:
If one internally feels weary of and seeks [liberation], one will naturally encounter a Buddha;
how could there be a lack of conditions?
If the conditions for perceiving a Buddha are met, the mind is free from defilement.
How is it that the cause is lacking?
Answer: Although there is internal weariness and seeking, [the cause is absent].
If one lacks the karmic activity of seeing the Buddha, it is because the mind has impurities;
thus, the condition is lacking.
If one possesses the karmic activity of meeting the Buddha yet gives rise to delight without a heart of insatiable seeking, then the cause is lacking.
These four lines should be contemplated according to reason.

To cause them to abandon evil and follow wholesome conduct by explaining what will be beneficial;

"Thus, from external conditions up to equal conditions. Commentary:
Next, regarding the distinctions among conditions, there are three parts presented therein:
the heading, the enumeration, and the explanation.

If they are explained individually,
there are six meanings based upon them.
First, the distinction of faculties (*indriya-viśeṣa*);
the treatise states that this person is distinguished from ordinary and inferior beings.
Second, the distinction of persons (*pudgala-viśeṣa*).

There are three distinctions in characteristics: first, the distinction from the initial generation of the resolve until the attainment of Buddhahood; second, the distinction of seeing; and third, the distinction of mindfulness. These are the differences in their respective characteristics.
4. Differentiation of conditions (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*):
because of the differentiation of conditions such as those of parents and so forth.
5. Differentiation of practice (*caryā-viśeṣa*).
Because they gather [beings] individually through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
there are six distinctions of benefit;
for the benefits differ according to whether one sees or hears them.
Regarding the condition of equality,
there are also six meanings.
The first is the person who is equal.
Because all dharmas are the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas;
second, the vow of equality,
because one vows to deliver all sentient beings without distinction.
Third, the mind of equality,
because it naturally perfumes [the continuum] and is never abandoned.
Fourth, equal practice.
The power of the knowledge of the identity [of all things] constitutes the essence of practice;
the fivefold equal benefit consists in manifesting activity according to the needs of those who see or hear it.
Sixth is the equality of capacity;
because one relies on the equality of insight through samādhi,
although there are six meanings, [they are unified].
The essentials consist of two points:
first, in terms of the capacity of the recipient;
second, in terms of the conditions.
Regarding the summary of conditions:
the transformation body has many gates, which are termed "differentiation";
the fundamental body accords with its nature, which is termed "equality."
Regarding the summary of the capacities:
that which is seen by the distracted mind is called "differentiation," while that which is seen by the concentrated mind is called "equality."
Within these two meanings, there are further two meanings:
equality and differentiation,
and differentiation and equality.
Regarding "equality and differentiation":

this refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally gather and benefit all beings without distinguishing between enemy and friend, yet manifest according to the differences of their faculties and the differences of their circumstances.
Regarding "differentiation and equality": [this refers to...]

First, he wishes to cause them to bear his kindness and to manifest shame for their own lack of it, thereby gathering living beings through affectionate kinship;

The *Xinlun* (New Treatise) states that below this there are further six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) intended to encompass the nurturing of living beings;
their meaning is identical to the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*). From "even unto" onwards, the specific categories are subsumed to form a general whole.

It is solely through sentient beings that Buddhas [attain their goal];
therefore, it is said that great compassion universally gathers and benefits all.

Regarding "spontaneous equality," it means that [the Buddha] constantly acts in accordance with the capacities of beings through effortless, natural cultivation, which is perpetually uninterrupted.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of being of the same essence" (*samatā-sarvātman*), this reveals its functional characteristic (*kāritra-lakṣaṇa*).
Because the essence of oneself and others is identical, it is termed "of the same essence."
The wisdom that knows this sameness is called the wisdom of the same essence (*samatā-jñāna*),
because it attains the state of equality with all sentient beings;
thus, it seeks to extinguish the suffering of others just as it extinguishes its own.
Suffering can be seen and heard;
because one sees and hears it for oneself, it naturally perfumes [the mind] accordingly, and so forth.

"Regarding what is called 'sentient beings reaching the point of seeing all Buddhas'":

thus, those above the stage of the Three Worthies, by the power of samādhi, all behold the Buddhas.

first, their characteristics are set forth.

Within the text, the two types of perfuming should be analyzed through four propositions.
That which has no beginning but has an end refers to fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodhi*).
Because it acts as the root of all defilements and is severed upon the attainment of Buddhahood,
it has a beginning and an end; that is to say, at its final stage, there is non-awakening.
Because it arises from the fundamental source and is severed through the attainment of Buddhahood,
it is without beginning and without end;
this refers to the nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*).
Because its nature is inherently and eternally true, without change or cessation,
it has a beginning but no end; this refers to the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi-jñāna*).
Because it manifests from the Truth and its essence is true and eternal,
there are two kinds of "beginninglessness":
in terms of time and in terms of arising.
Ignorance possesses both [aspects],
while the secondary branches possess only one;
since all are designated as defiled.
Therefore, it is said that defiled phenomena have been perfumed uninterruptedly since beginningless time;
this clarifies the two preceding phrases concerning defilement.
Both the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) are termed pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma*).
Because there is a beginning of its arising, it is not said to be beginningless;
because all things are without end, it is called "without interruption.
Therefore, it is said that the perfuming of pure dharmas is uninterrupted, and so forth.
This refers to the manifestation of the two subsequent pure [bodies].
If that were so, it would contradict the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*,
for that scripture states that while the *dharmakāya* for one's own benefit begins at a specific point, the *nirmāṇakāya* for the benefit of others has no beginning.
Answer: This teaching speaks of "having a beginning" because initial enlightenment (ādikṣaya-bodhi) exists in dependence upon fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi);
that teaching speaks of "having no beginning" because initial enlightenment is identical to fundamental enlightenment.
This [text] states that because fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) is primordially and eternally present, it is said to be "without beginning.
That [text] states that because the Dharma-body (dharma-kāya) is manifested only upon severing hindrances, it is said to be "attained for the first time.
Each is based on a single aspect of meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another.
For this reason, it is non-beginning yet beginning, and beginning yet non-beginning;
it is the beginning of that which has no beginning, and the non-beginning of that which begins.
All are without obstruction.

this body is said to be the Dharma-body; only the wisdom that accords with suchness (tathatā) is called the Dharma-body and so forth.
Therefore, the Dharma-body alone is free from purposeful activity;
although the sublime wisdom of ultimate truth is primordially and eternally serene,
it responds to the capacities of sentient beings, providing boundless benefit through its functional manifestations.
Just as water is itself the waves and itself the stillness, its function is constant;
therefore, according to sentient beings, it is described as having "function" and so forth.

it will be explained separately below;

Treatise:

There are two parts to the following explanation.
The first part correctly reveals the characteristics of its function;
the latter consists of questions and answers that resolve doubts.
Within the former, there are also two sections.
First, the meaning is directly revealed;
second, it is restated and analyzed.
Within the first part, there are again two sections.
First, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is elucidated; subsequently, the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) will be revealed.
This is the first [section].
The text consists of two sections.
The first reveals the coarse physical marks perceived by ordinary beings and followers of the Two Vehicles when they behold the Buddha.
This is seen based on the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of discriminating objects).
This consciousness does not know that all objects are merely mind;
it clings to the existence of external objects and gives rise to discrimination.
Relying on this coarse consciousness, one discriminates the Buddha-body and perceives only the marks of the coarse form of the *nirmāṇakāya*,
but does not see the subtle and wondrous form-marks of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Therefore, that which is seen is called the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Because [beings] do not know the reason why they perceive what is coarse—as explained below—they are deluded regarding the fact that appearances are mind-only; thus it is said that [the object] comes from "outside."
This means that the Buddha comes from the Tuṣita Heaven;
furthermore, it refers to the Buddha’s physical form, which does not reach beyond the limits of materiality.
"Marks" refers to the Buddha’s physical characteristics.
However, the sixteen-foot [form] and so forth are merely the limits of delusion;
the characteristics of form have no such limits.
Therefore, this is called "not knowing exhaustively."
Regarding the manifestation of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), there are many interpretations. According to one view:
The evolving consciousnesses are the first seven;
that is to say, these seven consciousnesses are able to give rise to delusive objects,
just as one perceives [floating] flowers and so forth in the pure sky.
Now, because one falsely perceives the Buddha-body through this consciousness,
it is said that [the Buddha] manifests in dependence upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This is because the Buddha is exclusively the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
"It is merely what is falsely perceived by the evolving consciousnesses.
According to another interpretation, the reasoning stated previously is not established.
It is therefore said that because they lack the benefit of others,
the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is also able to manifest illusory objects;
it is not only the preceding seven that are called evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This refers to the second of the three subtle states of the ālayavijñāna, specifically its "evolving aspect" (pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa).
It is intended to demonstrate that the Buddha-body arises from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna);
thus, any one of these three subtle states may be cited.
This means that for those who see the Buddha, there are causes and conditions.
The conditions refer to the power of the great compassionate vows of all Buddhas;
the causes refer to the seeds of goodness within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) of sentient beings.
The seeds of consciousness are struck and activated by the conditions of compassionate vows;
thus, within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the Buddha-body is manifested.
In other contexts, based on conditions alone, it is merely said that the Buddha manifests the physical forms of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*.
This is stated solely from the perspective of the cause; thus, it is said that [the ālayavijñāna] manifests in dependence upon the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna).
According to one interpretation, this explanation is not yet fully comprehensive or clear in its reasoning.
The transformation of the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) may indeed be logically tenable; however,
the explanation regarding the causes and conditions for seeing the Buddha relies on the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa),
and thus does not manifest the principle of the union of the real and the false.
Since this consciousness is a synthesis of the true and the false,
it is said that the Buddha-body manifests at this stage;
this is intended to reveal that [the manifestation] occurs through the causal conditions of the true and the false.
The "cause" refers to the pure, true essence of sentient beings;
the "condition" refers to the deluded thoughts of ignorance of sentient beings.
The true mind of sentient beings and the essence of the Buddha are non-dual.
Because of the confusion caused by forgetfulness and delusion,
at that time True Suchness merely conforms to the appearance of defilement and its pure function is not manifest.
Through the internal permeation of original enlightenment (mūla-awakening), it causes ignorance to give rise to a mind of weary detachment and seeking within that false consciousness.
Because there is a desire for cessation, the true function immediately manifests;
because the desire for cessation is weak, the characteristics of its function are coarse. As the desire for cessation gradually increases, [the function becomes increasingly subtle].
As the characteristics [of the mind] are transformed,
they become increasingly subtle. In this way, gradually, until the ignorance at the source of the mind is exhausted,
both aversion and seeking come to rest entirely.
Initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) is identical to the fundamental function, which returns to the equality of the essence.
In this equality, there is neither duality nor distinction; how, then, could retributive forms or characteristics manifest?
Until one reaches the source of the mind, the characteristics of function and appearance manifest as coarse or subtle within consciousness according to the faculties [of the senses].
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-body manifests through the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-parāvṛtti*).
If this is so, and it is merely from the Truth (*tathatā*) that the Buddha manifests,
why is it said that he manifests through the transformation of consciousness?
Answer: Because True Suchness (tathatā) alone cannot manifest by itself, it is said that the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) manifest in conjunction with it.
This means that, following the flow of saṃsāra, there exists a delusive functional capacity.
Although the false has efficacy, it cannot be established apart from the true;
if one turns back the outflow, the true possesses functional power.
Although the true has efficacy, it is not manifested apart from the false.
Therefore, the manifestation of the true Buddha must necessarily rely upon false conditions;
thus, its function is described in terms of their conjunction.
If this is so, then since it is the true function of one's own mind, how can it be called the Buddha’s recompense or transformation body?
Answer: Because the true mind of sentient beings is the very essence of all Buddhas.
As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states in this verse:
If anyone wishes to know all the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
they should compose this *Tathāgata-anutpāda-anuccheda-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Non-increase and Non-decrease of All Tathāgatas).
Furthermore, it says:
The Dharma-body is precisely sentient beings;
sentient beings are precisely the Dharma-body.
The meanings of "Dharma-body" and "sentient beings" are one in substance but differ only in name.
Since the various bodies of reality (dharmakāya) give rise to the functions of the recompense and transformation bodies,
why are they not the minds of sentient beings? If that were so,
then mind, Buddha, and sentient beings would be self-created.
Why is it said that the Buddha’s power of compassionate vow? Answer:
This very true mind is itself the Buddha’s compassionate vow.
This means that the minds of sentient beings and the Buddhas are non-dual.
Since the compassionate vows of all Buddhas arise based on the Truth (tathatā),
they likewise reside within the true mind of sentient beings.
When sentient beings weary of [suffering] and seek liberation,
the true function [of the Buddha-nature] manifests; how could this not be the compassionate vow of the Buddha?
This is precisely the unconditioned great compassion arising from the nature (*dharmatā-utpatti*) and the vow that is non-obstructive by its very essence.
If this is so, why do sentient beings, who have possessed minds since beginningless time, not awaken early and employ it to extinguish ignorance?
Answer: Because true permeation lacks power and one has not yet developed weariness with or a desire for [the mundane].
If that is so, since original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) already exists from the outset, [how can it be said to arise?]
"Why do you not cultivate [the mind] early on so as to bring about weariness with [samsara] and the desire for liberation? Answer:
"Because the nature of ignorance varies according to its thickness or thinness."
Because causes and conditions may be mutually deficient either before or after.
If that were so, and the true mind itself were the Buddha,
how could it be said that one attains Buddhahood by cultivating causes?
Answer: Because there is a distinction between original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) and initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).
If one speaks from the perspective of original enlightenment following defilement, the mind of sentient beings is itself called the Buddha.
However, as for initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), it is also produced through cultivation until it reaches the source of the mind, where all is equal and of one single limit.
How could there be any distinction such that it is said to arise from [cultivation]?
Treatise:
Second, that which relies on the ultimate is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. The commentary states:
The following clarifies the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Within this, there are three [aspects].
First, by means of consciousness, the person is raised to clarify what they perceive.
Next, the characteristics of the two types of retribution—the primary body and the environment—are revealed.
Finally, the name "retribution" is explained and clarified by showing how the result arises from its cause.

From the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) upward, all bodhisattvas transform that karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) into the wisdom of the perceiving subject (*darśana-jñāna*).
It is by relying on this wisdom that they behold the Buddha’s reward body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
Therefore, it is said that one sees based on the karmic consciousness;
it does not mean that the karmic consciousness itself is the seer,
for this consciousness is subtle and has not yet attained the capacity to see.
It is taught that through the power of ignorance, those karmic consciousnesses are transformed into deluded vision;
now, because they are transformed by true permeation into the wisdom capable of seeing,
it is said that one sees the Buddha based upon karma.
Treatise:
The body has immeasurable [qualities], up to immeasurable secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). Explanation:
The following reveals the marks of fruition (*vipākaphala-lakṣaṇa*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the primary retribution;
second, the environmental retribution.
This is the first [point].
Because the body has no boundaries, it is said to be "immeasurable in form.
This is based on the characteristics of the body.
The marks are also boundless;

Alternatively, it is because colors such as blue and yellow are not limited;
because within a single color there are boundless aspects;
and because within a single aspect there are infinite excellences.
Marks serve to manifest virtue, causing people to revere that virtue and mindfully recollect the Buddha.
Adorning the body serves to inspire love and joy, leading people to draw near.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha’s body possesses the primary and secondary marks.
Treatise:
"The fruit of reliance upon which one dwells, up to its being neither destroyed nor lost. Commentary:
This clarifies that it refers to the environmental retribution by using the term "fruit of reliance."
Because the pure land that serves as the basis and the primary retribution that depends upon it are boundless,
the resultant environment in which they reside is likewise endowed with immeasurable quantities of various flowers, such as the king of lotuses, and other such features.
The various supreme perfections of the Pure Land are thus further described as having diverse adornments that, in whatever manner they manifest, are all *tathatā* (suchness).
Their manifestation is immeasurable; hence it is said to be "without limit."
That which has no end or limit is called inexhaustible;
that which is mutually fused and unimpeded is called without boundaries.
Whatever marks are manifested according to the karmic actions one has performed, such they shall be.
That which is appropriate therein is eternally abiding;
it is not like the manifested lands where the three calamities actually destroy them.
Because evil persons suffer loss, it is said that [the merit] "dwells accordingly in the branches and so forth.
Treatise:
Such merits lead to the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Commentary:
This result is termed "fruition" (*vipāka*) because it is explained as arising from causes.
Thus, the characteristics of the fruition of the merits of the environment and its inhabitants— marvelous matters that are unobstructed and unhindered—
are all due to the permeation of the profound practice of the ten perfections.

Furthermore, because it is accomplished by the two causes—the internal and external—consisting of the inconceivable perfuming of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), and because its marks of bliss are perfectly complete, it is called "retribution" (*vipāka*).
Treatise:
Furthermore, from ordinary beings up to [the stage where] it is said to be the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). Commentary:

It was previously stated that the *saṃbhogakāya* is perceived by ordinary beings;

the present passage clarifies the distinctions regarding dreams in order to further elucidate the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, ordinary beings see [the Buddha] as equal [to themselves]," while the followers of the Two Vehicles see the Buddha as a supramundane body, such as the body of an Arhat or the body of a golden man.
As for what ordinary beings see, it varies according to the six realms of existence.
Those in hell see the Buddha as the foot of a black elephant; those belonging to the class of *rūpa-dhātu* (form-realm beings) see him as a body three feet tall;
non-Buddhist outsiders see him as one whose body is smeared with ashes, and so forth.
Furthermore, Tiwei and others see him through the virtues of humans and devas as a spirit, a celestial immortal (*deva-rṣi*), and so on.
Accordingly, what is perceived by each of the six realms of existence differs;
none of these are the supramundane commonality of the Truth of Suffering.
Therefore, they are termed "the aspect of not experiencing happiness."
The fruit does not correspond to the cause;
it is not a retribution for external causes.
Rather, it is spoken of as "correspondence" (pratirūpa) because it manifests in accordance with the person.
Treatise:
From the bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment until the stage of the dharma-body. Commentary:
The following clarifies the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Within this, there are two parts:

This is the first [section].

By relying on the gate of contemplation through inference, one perceives the principle of *tathatā* (suchness);

Because it differs from the preceding ten stages of faith, it is described as "profound."
Because it is a true realization distinct from what follows, it is simply called "faith.
The phrase "knowing those" clarifies the aspect of partial vision.
Because one perceives that True Suchness (tathatā) differs from that of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle,
one knows that the Buddha’s bodies and lands have no coming or going;

Because there is no deluded mind that comes or goes,
though there is coming, there is nowhere from which it comes;
because it arises from delusive confusion, there is no wisdom and no destination to which it goes.
"Non-separation from True Suchness explains the absence of boundaries": since those material forms are not separate from True Suchness, they are all equal to True Suchness and thus lack boundaries.
This describes the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) as perceived prior to the [ten] stages (bhūmi).
When the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises speak of "seeing on the stages" (*bhūmi*),

they refer to the state of accomplishment through the attainment of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) and its corresponding meditative application (*samprayoga*), wherein one directly realizes suchness (*tathatā*) from the first stage onward.

Here, however, we speak of "partial seeing" (*kiṃcid-darśana*) based on the stage prior to the [first] stage (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), which refers to partial seeing through the corresponding inferential contemplation (*anumāna-vipaśyanā*).
Since this is not yet true insight,
it does not conflict with that [state];
it merely differs from the limited mind of ordinary beings in that it does not seek the Buddha externally.
This briefly reveals the aspect of "seeing" based on a small portion of Mind-Only;
however, that this bodhisattva still engages in conceptual discrimination serves to distinguish them from bodhisattvas on the [ten] stages (bhūmi).
Because one attains profound understanding by relying on contemplation,

"If one attains a pure mind up to the point of perceiving contrary characteristics. The commentary states:
